Jazz is an American musical genre born in early twentieth-century New Orleans, fusing African American blues, ragtime, and European harmonic traditions with a culture of collective improvisation. Centered on swing rhythm and syncopation, it became the defining popular music of the mid-century and one of America's most profound cultural exports, transforming music performance itself by turning the soloist's spontaneous invention into an art form equal to composed melody.

Jazz emerged in New Orleans around 1900, where Caribbean, African, and European musical traditions collided in a port city of unusual cultural hybridity. Early practitioners adapted European instruments like trumpet, trombone, and clarinet and used classical harmonic structures to play blues and ragtime idioms. The birth of jazz coincides with the end of slavery's legal structures and the rise of Black autonomous cultural institutions—dance halls, saloons, and brass bands where self-taught and formally trained musicians improvised together. The Original Dixieland Jazz Band, a white ensemble, made the first jazz recordings in 1917, but Black New Orleans musicians including Buddy Bolden on cornet, Jelly Roll Morton on piano, and King Oliver on cornet had already established the style in live performance.

Improvisation is the essence of jazz. Unlike classical music, jazz is partly composed and partly invented in real time, with musicians responding to harmonic changes and one another's ideas. Syncopation and swing rhythm—an off-beat accent and elasticity that defies strict metronomic time—are jazz's rhythmic signature, derived from African polyrhythm and blues phrasing. The blues scale and blue notes, the flattened third and seventh degrees, permeate jazz tonality and give the music its characteristic bent quality, distinct from European diatonic scales. The typical jazz ensemble was small: a front line of trumpet, trombone, and clarinet played melodic ideas over a rhythm section of piano, upright bass, and drums, with all voices improvising simultaneously in a technique called New Orleans polyphony.

Jazz developed through distinct eras. Early jazz, from 1900 through the nineteen-twenties, featured collective improvisation in New Orleans style, focused on blues and ragtime idioms; Jelly Roll Morton was a master composer in this era. The swing era of the nineteen-thirties and nineteen-forties brought big bands with arranged harmonies that provided frameworks for soloists. Duke Ellington and Count Basie led orchestras that swung, while Louis Armstrong rose to fame as a trumpet soloist and vocalist. Bebop in the nineteen-forties was a revolutionary style led by Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, and Thelonious Monk, featuring faster tempos, complex chord changes, and asymmetrical melodic lines that shifted focus from ensemble swing to individual virtuosity. Cool jazz in the nineteen-fifties reacted to bebop's intensity, emphasizing cerebral arrangement and modal harmony; Miles Davis recorded Kind of Blue in 1959, a landmark modal jazz album that influenced generations. Free jazz and modal jazz from the nineteen-sixties onward saw John Coltrane and Ornette Coleman push past fixed chord changes; the genre fragmented into countless substyles—fusion, soul jazz, avant-garde.

Jazz reshaped Western music itself; its emphasis on individual voice and spontaneous dialogue influenced classical composers like George Gershwin and Aaron Copland, popular song, and global music traditions. It became a symbol of American freedom and creativity during the Cold War, despite and because of its roots in Black struggle; jazz tours were sponsored as cultural diplomacy. Today, jazz is a global music, with thriving scenes in Europe, Japan, Brazil, and beyond, taught in universities as both history and performance practice, a canonized high art. Jazz stands unique as a democratizing force: a music created by people denied access to formal conservatory training, yet so powerful it redefined how Western music is made. Unlike the composer-performer divide of classical music, jazz insisted on real-time creation—the performer as a co-composer. This challenged the notion that true art requires advance composition and rigid rehearsal, and it emerged from the Blues tradition, itself a repository of African American resilience and vernacular wisdom. The swing rhythm, the blue note, the soloist's primacy—these represent a different conception of musical beauty: one that values spontaneity, communal response, and the unique voice of the individual player.
